message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
The proposal has two parts, both from 1 June:
- raise the weekend Best Available Rate from £145 to £165, worth a projected £204,000 a year;
- introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday.

It argues that last June's £10 rise showed weekend guests aren't sensitive to price, and calls the £204,000 a floor.

The case that we're priced below the competition is sound. But the price-sensitivity evidence comes from a comparison distorted by season. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count and applies the increase to bookings that won't pay it. And the two-night minimum collides with the wedding business that the paper itself describes.

## 1. The June-to-July rise reflects the season, not price

- The paper's evidence is that occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July after the £10 increase.
- But Table 1 shows that **July and August are the hotel's busiest months every year**, driven by the harbour festival and school holidays. The paper says so itself in §2.
- A rise from June to July is expected whatever the price. Occupancy had also *fallen* from May (85%) to June (81%) before the increase.
- **A fair test** compares July 2025 with July 2024 at the old rate, and ideally with the competitive set's occupancy over the same months.
- **The value-for-money score of 8.4 was measured at £145.** It shows guests are happy at that price, not that they'll stay as happy at £165.

So the paper hasn't shown that guests aren't sensitive to price. That doesn't mean they are. The rate gap to competitors is a real argument for an increase. The question is open, not decided against the proposal.

## 2. The revenue figure is overstated and isn't a floor

**The room count is wrong.** §2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**; §5 calculates with **124**.

| Rooms | Calculation | Annual gain |
|---|---|---|
| 124 (as used) | 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 | £203,800 |
| **112 (as stated in §2)** | 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 | **£184,000** |

**Not every booking pays the new rate.** The £20 is applied to every occupied weekend room. But §6 honours corporate rates and contracted group rates. Wedding blocks, around 38% of Saturday rooms, are likely group bookings. Only rooms sold at the published rate gain the £20. The paper needs the share of weekend rooms that are actually sold at the published rate.

**Holding occupancy at 2025 levels isn't "conservative."** It assumes a 14% price rise has no effect on demand, which is exactly what §1 failed to show.

**Commission and VAT may also apply.** Online travel agents take commission on their bookings, and UK room rates include VAT. If the £204,000 is gross revenue, net room revenue is lower.

## 3. The two-night minimum conflicts with wedding business

§4 says wedding guests make up **about 38% of Saturday bookings**, and they typically **arrive Saturday and leave Sunday**. Those are exactly the one-night Saturday stays the minimum targets.

- If wedding blocks are exempt, the minimum doesn't touch the largest group of single-night Saturday guests.
- If they aren't exempt, couples' guests are forced to pay for a second night or to stay elsewhere. That risks losing the business and harming the relationship with Quayside Hall.
- The paper doesn't say which. This needs deciding before launch.

**The minimum can also lose revenue, so the £204,000 isn't a floor.**
- On the 31 sold-out Saturdays, guests who want one night may book elsewhere rather than add a night. If two-night demand doesn't fill their place, Saturday rooms go unsold.
- On the other 21 Saturdays, the minimum simply turns away people who wanted one night.
- Hotels often apply minimum stays only on dates expected to sell out, with group blocks exempt. That would limit the risk.

## 4. The monitoring trigger is reasonable, with one caveat

- The price rise still pays for itself on room revenue unless occupancy falls by about 12% in relative terms, since 145 ÷ 165 = 0.88. At 79% occupancy, that's about 9–10 points.
- A trigger of 5 points below 2025 is therefore a sensible early warning.
- **Caveat:** if the two-night minimum shifts Saturday demand to other hotels, the occupancy figure will mix that effect with the price effect. Track Saturday single-night bookings that are turned away, and wedding block pick-up, separately.

## 5. Further points

- **Positioning.** £165 is the *bottom* of the competitor range (£165–180). After the change, the hotel is no longer priced below the competition; it's level with the cheapest competitor. That may be right for a four-star hotel, but say so explicitly.
- **Timing.** Rates are loaded on 15 May for stays from 1 June. Many June weekend rooms will already have been booked at £145, so 2026's gain will be lower than a full-year figure suggests.

## 6. What holds up

- **The rate gap:** £20–35 below three comparable hotels is a genuine reason to raise prices.
- **The 2025 average:** weekend occupancy of 79% is correct, and is the sum of the months ÷ 12.
- **Saturday demand:** 31 sold-out Saturdays shows that demand is strong on many dates.
- **Weekly monitoring** against the same weeks last year is the right comparison. It's the year-on-year approach that §3 should have used.
- **Contracted rates are protected.**

## 7. What is settled and what is open

**Settled by the paper's own figures:**
- the June-to-July rise reflects the season and says nothing about price sensitivity;
- the revenue calculation uses 124 rooms against a stated 112;
- the paper doesn't resolve how the two-night minimum interacts with one-night wedding stays.

**Open, and what would settle each question:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| How sensitive weekend guests are to price | July 2025 v July 2024, alongside the competitive set's figures |
| How many weekend rooms gain the £20 | The share of weekend rooms sold at the published rate |
| Whether wedding blocks are exempt | A decision, ideally agreed with Quayside Hall |
| Net effect of the two-night minimum | A trial on selected high-demand dates only |

## 8. Suggested revision to the recommendation

> We recommend raising the weekend BAR from £145 to £165 from 1 June, bringing it level with the lower end of our competitive set. On 112 rooms, if every occupied weekend room paid the new rate and occupancy held at 2025 levels, this would add up to £184,000 a year. The realised figure will be lower in proportion to the share of weekend rooms sold at contracted corporate or group rates. We recommend applying the two-night Saturday minimum only on dates forecast to sell out, with wedding and group blocks exempt, and reviewing it after three months.

I can build a revenue table showing results at different shares of published-rate bookings and different occupancy levels, if that would help.
